transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Head of AI, Regatta), Liam O'Neill (Infra Eng, Regatta), Sophie Zhang (CISO, Regatta)

Summary (auto): Regatta is evaluating dedicated reserved capacity for inference. Primary drivers are data isolation, cost predictability, and latency SLOs for customer-facing features. They want to understand commit tiers, burst behavior, and security/compliance fit.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya, i'm the account exec on the redwood side. um quick intro from us, jonas is our systems se who will take the deep dive, and then over to you, aisha, feel free to intro the team
[00:12] Aisha: hey maya, hey jonas, thanks. i'm aisha, head of ai at regatta capital. with me liam infra and sophie our ciso. we're evaluating options for production inference for our portfolio of models, thinking dedicated capacity but want to validate tradeoffs
[00:25] Jonas: great, thanks. quick agenda: sizing and commit tiers, isolation/networking, burst/autoscale, perf/latency, security, next steps. anything to add?
[00:32] Liam: nope that's good; also interested in how you handle model variants and fallback when capacity is constrained
[00:38] Maya: yep we'll cover routing and fallbacks
[00:42] [02:05] Jonas: to start, can you share rough qps and model sizes? that drives GPU counts and commit tiers
[02:12] Aisha: yes, so two main models: a 13b seq2seq we use for summarization, and a 70b decoder for high-quality generation for client-facing emails. peak traffic for the 13b is about 250 qps during batch windows, sustained 60 qps; 70b is lower, peak 30 qps but latency sensitive. seq lengths average 512 tokens for summaries, emails often 256 but bursts up to 1024
[02:40] Jonas: ok helps. for Dedicated we typically size pools by model family and expected concurrency; rough rule of thumb for 13b at that qps would be X GPUs depending on quant and batching. we can propose M series or A100 based on quantization. question: do you plan to quantize 70b?
[03:02] Aisha: we want to keep quality for the 70b; maybe 8-bit quant but not aggressive 4-bit for now
[03:08] Jonas: understood. so commit tiers - we offer monthly reserved capacity with burst windows to shared capacity. commit levels map to dedicated GPU counts and guaranteed throughput. bursts go to our shared pool or to larger GPUs if configured. important to discuss isolation: do you need fully private (air-gapped) or is VPC plus customer-managed keys enough?
[03:28] Sophie: for now VPC + customer-managed KMS is mandatory; full on-prem air gap is a future ask but not today. we also need audit logs retained 13 months and SSO/SAML integration
[03:39] Maya: we support KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, SAML SSO and retention options. we'll include the security pack.
[03:47] [05:10] Liam: can you explain how burst actually works? e.g., if we commit to 8 GPUs but see sudden spike, how quickly do you scale and what's the cost model for burst?
[05:18] Jonas: good question. burst is two tiers: short-term burst to shared hosted capacity - that's immediate but subject to spot-like availability and slightly higher per-token cost; second tier is pre-warmed burst nodes in the same dedicated pool you can purchase as standby for predictable bursts. autoscaling policies let you set min/max and burst window. typical warm-up is a few seconds for extra nodes when model weights are hot, kv cache warm-up can add latency.
[05:40] Aisha: that kv cache comment - for our email flow we have strong latency requirements, something like 200-400ms end-to-end for 70b is our goal. how realistic is that on dedicated?
[05:52] Jonas: 200-400ms for a 70b is challenging but achievable with optimized kernels, smaller batch sizes, and reserved latency-critical capacity. we generally reserve low-latency lanes with pre-warmed kv caches and pin models to nodes. if you need that SLO at scale it requires more reserved GPUs relative to pure throughput sizing.
[06:12] [07:30] Sophie: from security side: KMS is required, also separation of logs per tenant, SOC 2 type II attestations, and ability to restrict egress from nodes. do you support host-level RBAC and audit trail on prompts / tokens?
[07:45] Maya: yes on SOC 2 - we have attestations. we support KMS for key wrapping, and customers can choose retention windows for logs. prompts can be logged or omitted; RBAC across console and APIs is supported. we will share the security pack with exact controls and certs
[08:05] Liam: what's the network architecture? will our VPC peer or is it private-link style?
[08:12] Jonas: we offer VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink depending on region. for completely private deployments we support Private (customer-managed control plane) or an on-prem package for air-gapped cases. both give you network isolation, but Private has a slightly different upgrade cadence
[08:30] [09:45] Aisha: commercial question - how does pricing change if we buy more reserved GPUs vs rely on burst? we want predictable unit cost per token without huge surprises
[09:55] Maya: committed capacity is lower per-token, predictable monthly fee; burst to shared capacity is metered at higher per-token rate. we can show an example spreadsheet with per-GPU commit tiers and effective per-token math at different utilization levels. i'll include typical utilization assumptions and amortized infra cost in the sheet
[10:15] Jonas: also note quantization changes that math - 4-bit can cut GPU count in half for some models, but you indicated you want to preserve quality for 70b so you'll get less from quant there
[10:27] [12:00] Liam: on the ops side, how do you handle model rollouts and canarying? we need automated rollbacks and A/B testing per endpoint
[12:08] Jonas: Redwood supports rollouts: canary percent, A/B, and automatic fallback to alternative model variants if latency or error thresholds breach. routes can be weighted and you can pin model versions. metrics and tracing hooks are available in the console and via APIs
[12:28] Aisha: great. do you provide token-level cost breakdowns per route so product managers can see which features cost the most?
[12:35] Maya: yes we have per-route cost and latency dashboards and we can export reports.
[12:40] [14:05] Sophie: i want to dive into keys: does redwood hold customer keys or do you support customer-managed HSM? also any side channels for prompt leakage?
[14:15] Jonas: we support customer-managed KMS and integration with HSM providers; by default keys are never exfiltrated. prompts remain in the node memory during inference; you can opt-out of logging prompts. we can also show architecture diagrams for key lifecycle and encryption at rest/in transit
[14:38] Sophie: ok i'd like those diagrams in the pack
[14:42] [16:20] Aisha: another question - what's your typical lead time for provisioning dedicated pools and for scaling up? if we sign a 6 or 12 month commit how quickly can you add GPUs?
[16:30] Jonas: provisioning time is region-dependent and depends on capacity, but for standard regions typical lead time is 3-10 business days for additional reserved GPUs; for urgent bursts we can use shared capacity immediately. if you need guaranteed expansion SLAs we can bake that into enterprise agreements
[16:50] Liam: and how do you handle hardware heterogeneity? do you mix A100s and H100s in the same pool?
[16:58] Jonas: we try to keep pools homogeneous per model to avoid performance variance. we can create mixed pools but routing logic will prefer compatible variants; if you want consistent latency we recommend homogeneous fleets for a given model version
[17:14] [18:40] Maya: any concerns on compliance/regulatory constraints?
[18:45] Sophie: primary is audit log retention, SSO & RBAC, KMS, and proof of no data exfil. also data residency - we need logs and keys to stay in eu region for specific models used with eu customers
[18:58] Jonas: we support region pinning and regional dedicated deployments; keys can be region-local. we'll call that out in the security pack
[19:10] [20:30] Aisha: last technical - do you support continuous KV or prefix caching across requests for conversational style workloads? we rely on cache to reduce cost for repeated contexts
[20:40] Jonas: yes, continuous prefix/KV caching is supported; it's configurable per route and can accelerate repeated context calls. caching interacts with autoscaling because warm caches matter for latency
[20:55] [22:50] Liam: for benchmark planning, what's the best sample we should provide? sequence length distribution, sample QPS, example prompts?
[22:58] Jonas: ideal: a 48-hour representative trace or a synthetic workload with a distribution: 60% 13b summaries at 512 tokens, 30% 70b emails at 256-1024 tokens, include typical prompt templates and any special plugins or tool calls. provide lat targets and we will run end-to-end with telemetry
[23:20] Aisha: we can provide that. pricing sample would be helpful to compare hosted vs dedicated at our utilization numbers
[23:27] Maya: noted. we'll model both.
[23:30] [25:00] Sophie: one more - in a failure scenario where dedicated pool goes down, is there an automated fallback to hosted? we need fail-open or fail-closed discussion
[25:10] Jonas: yes you can configure fallback policies: failover to hosted or alternative model family; you can also set to fail closed. we'll show example runbooks and SLO breach behaviors
[25:27] [27:05] Aisha: ok sounds good. want to recap next steps?
[27:12] Maya: recap: i'll send pricing and tiers + security pack (SOC 2 certs, KMS/HSM notes, network diagrams) by 2026-10-01/02. jonas and liam will coordinate a benchmark session week of 2026-10-05. sophie will compile any compliance questions and send them to maya by 2026-10-04.
[27:34] Liam: yep i'll pair with jonas to schedule the test and share infra access for telemetry collection
[27:40] Sophie: i'll assemble the compliance list
[27:45] Jonas: i'll prepare a perf test plan and a proposed dedicated sizing doc and bring recommended commit tiers to the benchmark
[27:55] [30:00] Maya: great thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links. any last quick q's?
[30:06] Aisha: none from me, thanks
[30:08] Liam: all good
[30:10] Sophie: thanks
[30:12] Maya: end.

Auto notes: references made to 'kv cache' and 'KMS/HSM', occasional mis-transcriptions present (e.g., 'Redwood Dedicate' vs 'Redwood Dedicated'). Links shared: security pack (link to internal doc), pricing spreadsheet (link to internal drive) - maya will send.
